slides.title: Principles Of Concurrency
slides.body: Principles Of Concurrency

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Definition
Introduction to Concurrent Processes
What is Concurrency?
Concurrency in operating systems refers to the capability of an OS to handle more than one task or process at the same time, thereby enhancing efficiency and responsiveness
slides.notes: Now, let's begin with Concurrency. Concurrency is the ability of an operating system to handle multiple tasks at the same time. By managing several processes efficiently, it improves both the performance and responsiveness of the system.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Concurrent Processes
Concurrent processes are two or more processes that are in progress at the same time in a system For example Multiple applications running on smartphone simultaneously
Browser
Music Player
Messaging app
slides.notes: Next, let's understand concurrent processes. These are multiple processes that make progress during the same period of time. A common example is a smartphone running a browser, music player, and messaging app simultaneously, allowing you to use all of them without waiting for one to finish first.

slides.title: Concurrent Processes
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Kitchen analogy: Cooking multiple dishes at the same time, sharing the same tools and ingredients

slides.title: Single Processor
slides.body:
How Process Execute Together?
Single Processor (One CPU): Processes take turns executing very quickly, appears as if they run simultaneously (time-sharing)
Process 1
Process 2
Process 1
Process 2
slides.notes: Now, let's see how concurrency works on a single processor. Since there's only one CPU, it can execute only one process at a time. The operating system quickly switches between processes using time-sharing, creating the illusion that they're running simultaneously.

slides.title: Single Processor
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Analogy: A single chef cooking multiple dishes by switching between pots

slides.title: Multiple Processors
slides.body:
How Do Process Execute Together?
Multiple Processors (Multiple CPUs): Processes can run truly simultaneously, each CPU handles a different process
slides.notes: Moving on, in a multiple processor system, each CPU can execute a different process at the same time. This means processes run truly in parallel, improving performance and allowing multiple tasks to progress simultaneously.

slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Analogy: Multiple chefs cooking different dishes at the same time

slides.notes: Next, concurrent processes often need to share system resources, such as the CPU, memory, or I/O devices. For example, if two programs send documents to the same printer, the operating system coordinates access so both can use the shared resource correctly.

slides.title: Concurrent Processes
slides.body:
Types
Processes that work alone without affecting others
Characteristics:
Do their own work
Don't share data with others
One process doesn't affect another
No need for coordination
Execution doesn’t depend on other processes
Independent Processes
slides.notes: Now, let's first look at independent processes. These processes execute on their own without relying on or interacting with other processes. Since they don't share data or resources, one process has no impact on the execution of another, so no coordination is required.

slides.title: Concurrent Processes
slides.body:
Processes that work together and share things
Characteristics:
Share data or resources
One process can affect another
Need to coordinate to avoid problems
May give different results based on timing
Need rules to work properly together
Cooperating Processes
Types
slides.notes: Moving on, cooperating processes work together to accomplish a task. They often share data or resources, so the actions of one process can influence another. Because of this, they need proper coordination and synchronization to ensure everything works correctly and consistently.

slides.title: Concurrent Processes
slides.body:
Examples
Banking
Printing
File Sharing
Two people withdrawing from same account
Multiple documents sent to one printer
Multiple users editing same document
slides.notes: Next, let's look at some real-world examples. In banking, multiple users may access the same account. In printing, several documents can be sent to a single printer. Similarly, in file sharing, multiple users may work on the same document. These situations require proper coordination to avoid conflicts.

slides.body:
Why Does This Matter?

slides.body:

Importance
slides.notes: SO, the key difference is that independent processes don't require any synchronization because they don't share resources. In contrast, cooperating processes do share data or resources, so they need proper synchronization to prevent conflicts and ensure correct execution.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Principles of Concurrency
When multiple processes execute concurrently, proper rules are required to ensure correct and efficient execution, the main principles are
Mutual Exclusion 
Progress (No Deadlock)
Fairness (Bounded Waiting)
Synchronization
slides.notes: Now, when multiple processes run concurrently, they must follow certain principles to avoid conflicts and ensure correct execution. The four key principles we'll discuss are mutual exclusion, progress, fairness, and synchronization, each addressing a different aspect of coordinating concurrent processes.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Mutual Exclusion
Progress
Only one process can access a shared resource at a time
The system should always move forward, A process should not wait unnecessarily when the shared resource is available
Principles of Concurrency
slides.notes: Moving on, the first principle is Mutual Exclusion, which ensures that only one process can access a shared resource at any given time. The second is Progress, which means if the resource is free, a process shouldn't be kept waiting unnecessarily, allowing the system to continue executing efficiently.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Fairness
Synchronization
Every process gets a chance to access shared resources, no process waits forever
Processes are coordinated so they don’t interfere with each other
Principles of Concurrency
slides.notes: Next, Fairness ensures that every process eventually gets its turn to use a shared resource, preventing indefinite waiting. Finally, Synchronization coordinates multiple processes so they can safely share resources without interfering with each other's execution.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Why it matters?
Principles of Concurrency
slides.notes: Why these principles of concurrency matter ?

slides.title: Principles of Concurrency
slides.body:
Why It Matters?
Ensures data consistency when processes share resources
Guarantees fair access to processes
Prevents conflicts and mistakes caused by simultaneous access
slides.notes: these principles are essential because they help maintain correct and consistent data when resources are shared. They also ensure fair access for all processes and prevent errors that can occur when multiple processes try to access the same resource simultaneously.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Advantages 
Better Resource Utilization
Resources unused by one application can be used by others
Maximizes hardware efficiency
Reduces idle time for CPU and I/O devices
Running Multiple Applications
Execute several applications simultaneously
Enhanced user experience and productivity
slides.notes: Now, one major advantage of concurrency is that it lets users run multiple applications at the same time, making the system more responsive and productive. It also improves resource utilization by allowing the CPU and I/O devices to work on different tasks instead of remaining idle.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Better Performance
One application uses processor while another uses disk
Parallel execution reduces total completion time
Throughput increases significantly
Improved Response Time
System remains responsive during long operations
Users don't wait for sequential completion
Interactive applications perform better
Advantages
slides.notes: Moving on, concurrency improves response time by keeping the system responsive during long operations, so users don't have to wait for tasks to finish sequentially. This also helps interactive applications perform more smoothly. It also improves overall performance by allowing the CPU and other resources, like the disk, to work on different tasks simultaneously, reducing execution time and increasing throughput.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Fairness
Multiple users/processes get fair access to resources
Prevents monopolization of system resources
Advantages
slides.notes: Next, concurrency also promotes fairness by giving multiple processes a fair chance to access shared resources. This prevents any single process from holding a resource for too long, ensuring balanced and efficient resource utilization.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Challenges
 Race Conditions
Outcome depends on which process executes first
Can lead to incorrect or inconsistent data
Example: Two people updating the same bank account at the same time
slides.notes: Now, one common challenge in concurrency is a race condition. It occurs when multiple processes access or modify the same data at the same time, and the final result depends on the order in which they execute. For example, two people updating the same bank account simultaneously can lead to incorrect data if access isn't properly controlled.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Deadlock
Two or more processes wait forever for resources held by each other
System becomes unresponsive
Example: Two printers and two print jobs waiting for each other’s printer
Challenges
slides.notes: Next, another challenge is deadlock. It occurs when two or more processes keep waiting for resources held by each other, so none of them can proceed. As a result, the system becomes unresponsive. A common example is two print jobs, each waiting for a printer that the other process is holding.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Starvation
Low-priority processes may never get CPU time if higher-priority processes keep arriving
Challenges
slides.notes: Finally, starvation occurs when a process keeps waiting because higher-priority processes continuously get CPU time. If this continues indefinitely, the waiting process may never get a chance to execute.

slides.title: Starvation
slides.body:
Example
Background maintenance tasks always delayed because user applications keep running
Background maintenance tasks
User applications
2
1
slides.notes: Now, let's understand starvation with this example. Here, user applications have higher priority, so they keep getting CPU time. As a result, background maintenance tasks are repeatedly postponed and may never execute, which is exactly what starvation means.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Non-Atomic / Blocking
Some actions must finish fully before another process can use the resource
Partial execution or waiting can cause errors or delays
Example: Saving a file while another program edits it simultaneously
Challenges
slides.notes: Next, some operations must be completed without interruption. If another process accesses the same resource before the operation finishes, it can lead to incorrect results or delays. For example, editing a file while it's still being saved may cause inconsistent data.

slides.title: Concurrency
slides.body:
Performance Overhead
Switching between processes and coordinating them takes extra time
Running too many processes at once can slow the system down
Example: Running many applications simultaneously causing frequent context switching and slowing down the system
Challenges
slides.notes: Finally, concurrency also introduces performance overhead. Managing multiple processes and switching between them consumes CPU time. If too many processes run simultaneously, frequent context switching can reduce overall system performance instead of improving it.

slides.title: The Critical-Section Problem
slides.body: The Critical-Section Problem
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the The Critical-Section Problem

slides.title: Critical-Section Problem
slides.body:
Introduction
A critical section is a part of the program where a process accesses shared resources or modifies shared variables
Accesses shared resources
Process
Modifies shared variables
slides.notes: Now, let's introduce the Critical Section. It is the part of a program where a process accesses shared resources or modifies shared data. Since multiple processes may try to access the same resource, this section must be carefully controlled to avoid conflicts.

slides.title: Critical-Section Problem
slides.body:
Why Only One Process At A Time?
Only one process should execute in the critical section at a time
If multiple processes enter concurrently, data inconsistency or errors can occur
Critical section
Critical section
Process 1
Process 1
Process 2
Process 3
Process 4
slides.notes: Next, only one process should be allowed inside the critical section at a time. If multiple processes enter it simultaneously, they may modify the same shared data, leading to incorrect or inconsistent results. This is why controlling access to the critical section is so important.

slides.title: Critical-Section Problem
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes:
Multiple people sharing a printer: 
Only one person can print at a time
If two print together → documents get mixed

slides.title: Critical Section
slides.body:
Structure of a Process
Entry section
Exit section
Critical section
Remainder section
do
While (TRUE)
Request access to critical section
Access shared resources safely
Release control, allow others to enter
Code not involving shared resources
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the structure of a process around a critical section. A process first enters the entry section to request access, then executes the critical section where it safely uses shared resources. After finishing, it leaves through the exit section, allowing other processes to enter, and finally continues with the remainder section, which doesn't involve shared resources.

slides.title: Critical Section
slides.body:
Structure of a Process
Entry Section: Request permission, acquire necessary locks
Critical Section: Access and modify shared resources atomically
Exit Section: Release locks and signal other processes
Remainder Section: Non-critical code, can run concurrently
slides.notes: Moving on, each part has a specific role. The entry section requests access to the shared resource, the critical section performs the shared operation safely, the exit section releases access for other processes, and the remainder section contains normal code that can run without any synchronization.

slides.title: Critical Section Structure
slides.body:
Analogy
Entry:standing in line to use printer
Critical: printing document
Exit: leaving printer for next person
Remainder: doing other tasks not using printer
slides.notes: Next, think of using a shared printer. First, you wait in line to get access—that's the entry section. Then you print your document, which is the critical section. Once you're done, you leave the printer so others can use it, and finally continue with your other work, which is the remainder section.

slides.title: Critical Section Solution Requirements
slides.body:
1. Mutual Exclusion
Only one process can be in the critical section at a time
Prevents race conditions and data corruption
slides.notes: Now, the first requirement is Mutual Exclusion. It ensures that only one process is allowed to access the shared resource at any given time. This avoids simultaneous access, helping maintain correct data and preventing conflicts between processes.

slides.title: Critical Section Solution Requirements
slides.body:
2. Progress
If no process is in the critical section, a waiting process must be allowed to enter
No unnecessary waiting, system moves forward
slides.notes: Next, the second requirement is Progress. If the critical section is free, a waiting process should be allowed to enter without unnecessary delay. This ensures the system keeps moving forward efficiently.

slides.title: Critical Section Solution Requirements
slides.body:
3. Bounded Waiting (Fairness)
Each process has a maximum waiting time before entering the critical section
Prevents starvation and ensures fair resource access
slides.notes: Finally, the third requirement is Bounded Waiting, which ensures that every process gets an opportunity to enter the critical section within a reasonable time. This prevents any process from being left waiting indefinitely and promotes equitable access to shared resources.

slides.title: Race Condition
slides.body: Race Condition
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Race Condition

slides.title: Race Condition Example
slides.body:
Race Condition – Bank Account Example
Scenario: Two simultaneous withdrawals from same account
Initial Balance: $100
Process P1
Read balance: $100   
Calculate: 100+10=110     
Write balance: $110     
  Process P2
Read balance: $100
Calculate: 100-10=90
Write balance: $90
slides.notes: Now, let's see a race condition through a bank account example. Both processes read the same initial balance of $100 at nearly the same time. Since each updates the balance independently, one update overwrites the other, producing an incorrect final balance. This happens because both processes accessed the shared data simultaneously without proper synchronization.

slides.title: Race Condition Example
slides.body:
Problem
Correct final balance should account for serialization
Both processes read $100 before either writes!
Final balance could be $110 or $90 (incorrect!)
slides.notes: Next, the issue is that both processes read the old balance before either updates it. As a result, one update gets overwritten, leading to an incorrect final balance. To prevent this, the transactions must be serialized, allowing only one process to update the account at a time.

slides.title: Race Condition
slides.body:
Causes
Interleaving of operations
CPU switches between processes while they are executing
Non-atomic operations
Read-Modify-Write sequence is not executed as a single step
Shared data access
Multiple processes access the same variable/resource
No synchronization
Processes don’t coordinate access to shared resources
slides.notes: Now, let's understand what causes a race condition. It can happen when processes are interleaved due to CPU switching, when read-modify-write operations aren't atomic, when multiple processes share the same data, and when there's no synchronization to coordinate access to that shared resource.

slides.title: Real-World Impacts
slides.body:
Why It Matters ?
Banking Systems
Incorrect balances, transaction errors
Airline Reservations
Double booking of seats
Inventory Systems
Wrong stock count
Databases
Data corruption due to simultaneous updates
slides.notes: Finally, race conditions can have serious real-world consequences. In banking, they can cause incorrect account balances. In airline reservation systems, they may result in double booking. Inventory systems can show incorrect stock levels, and in databases, simultaneous updates can lead to data corruption.

slides.title: Real-World Impacts
slides.body:
How to Prevent Race Conditions
Dekker’s Algorithm
Peterson’s Algorithm
 Works for 2 processes, ensures mutual exclusion
Simpler, demonstrates mutual exclusion, progress, and fairness
Software-Based Solutions
slides.notes: Next, race conditions can be prevented using software-based solutions. Two well-known approaches are Dekker's Algorithm and Peterson's Algorithm. Both are designed for two processes, with Peterson's algorithm being simpler and ensuring mutual exclusion, progress, and fairness.

slides.title: Software Solution
slides.body: Software Solution
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Software Solution

slides.title: Peterson’s Algorithm
slides.body:
Introduction
Classic software solution to the critical section problem for 2 processes, using:
No hardware
Ensuring mutual exclusion
Race-free access
Safe coordination
Two processes, P0 and P1, share two variables:
flag[i] : Process i wants to enter
Callout: flag[] shows intent; turn breaks the tie when both want in at once
turn : Says whose turn it is to enter the critical section
slides.notes: Now, let's introduce Peterson's Algorithm, a classic software solution for the critical section problem involving two processes. It doesn't require any hardware support and ensures mutual exclusion with safe coordination. It uses two shared variables: flag[], which indicates a process wants to enter the critical section, and turn, which decides which process gets priority if both request access at the same time.

slides.title: Peterson's Solution - Pseudocode
slides.notes: Now, flag[i] = true indicates that Pi wants to enter the critical section. Next, turn = j gives priority to Pj if both request access together. The while condition checks whether Pj also wants to enter and waits if it's Pj's turn. Once the condition becomes false, Pi enters the critical section, sets flag[i] = false after finishing, and then continues with the remainder section before repeating the process.

slides.title: Peterson's Solution - Pseudocode
slides.notes: Similarly, the code for Process Pj works in exactly the same way. It sets flag[j] = true to request access, gives priority to Pi using turn = i, waits if needed, executes the critical section, resets flag[j] = false on exit, and then continues with the remainder of the program.

slides.title: Peterson's Solution
slides.body:
Why It Works?
Mutual Exclusion
Progress
Pi enters only when flag[j] == false or turn == i. Since turn can't be both 0 and 1, both processes can never be inside at once
if the other process doesn't want in (flag[j] == false), Pi enters immediately
slides.notes: For Mutual Exclusion, flag[j] and turn work together to ensure that if both processes request the critical section simultaneously, only Pi or Pj is allowed to enter.For Progress, whenever flag[j] is false, indicating the other process isn't interested, Pi can enter the critical section immediately without unnecessary waiting.

slides.title: Peterson's Solution
slides.body:
Why It Works?
Bounded waiting
The turn variable forces alternation, so a process waits at most one turn
slides.notes: Finally, Peterson's Algorithm also provides bounded waiting. The turn variable ensures that processes take turns fairly, so no process has to wait indefinitely before entering the critical section.

slides.title: Peterson's Algorithm
slides.body:
Both Want to Enter at Once
P0 sets flag[0]=true, turn=1; P1 sets flag[1]=true, turn=0
The last write to turn wins - say P1 wrote last → turn = 0
P0 enters (its condition turn==1 is now false)
P1 waits (both parts of its condition are true)
Exactly one enters → mutual exclusion holds
slides.notes: Now, let's consider the case where both P0 and P1 request the critical section at the same time. Both set their respective flag values to true and update the turn variable. The last write to turn determines which process gets priority. In this example, since turn = 0, P0 enters the critical section, while P1 waits. This guarantees that only one process enters at a time, satisfying Mutual Exclusion.

slides.title: Peterson's Algorithm
slides.body:
Limitations
Works for only two processes (doesn't scale directly to many)
Relies on atomic reads/writes and assumes instructions aren't reordered
Modern CPUs may reorder memory operations, so real systems use hardware primitives or OS tools instead
Mainly of conceptual and academic value - it clearly demonstrates the three requirements
slides.notes: Finally, Peterson's Algorithm has a few limitations.1  It works only for two processes and 2 assumes atomic operations with no instruction reordering. 3 Since modern processors may reorder memory operations, real operating systems rely on hardware synchronization mechanisms instead. 4 Today, Peterson's Algorithm is mainly used to understand the core principles of synchronization.

slides.title: Real-World Impacts
slides.body:
How to Prevent Race Conditions
Atomic instructions: Test-and-Set (TAS), Compare-and-Swap (CAS)
Disabling interrupts (only for uniprocessor systems)
Hardware-Based Solutions

slides.body:

OS-Level Solutions

Monitors

Condition variables

slides.title: Real-World Impacts
slides.body:
How to Prevent Race Conditions
Synchronized methods (Java), 
Atomic variables, 
Concurrent data structures
Language-Level Solutions

slides.title: Synchronization Hardware
slides.body: Synchronization Hardware
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Synchronization Hardware

slides.title: Synchronization Hardware
slides.body:
Introduction
Special CPU instructions that help solve the critical section problem efficiently
Provides atomic operations that cannot be interrupted
slides.notes: Now, let's move from software solutions to hardware-based synchronization. Modern processors provide special CPU instructions that perform operations atomically, meaning they cannot be interrupted. This makes solving the critical section problem much more efficient and reliable.

slides.title: Synchronization Hardware
slides.body:
Software-only solutions are often complex and slow
Hardware ensures fast, simple, and reliable mutual exclusion
Introduction
slides.notes: Next, compared to software-only approaches, hardware-based synchronization is much simpler and faster. By providing built-in atomic instructions, it offers a more reliable way to achieve mutual exclusion in modern systems.

slides.title: Synchronization Hardware
slides.body:
Execute completely or not at all (cannot be interrupted)
Forms the foundation of hardware-based synchronization primitives
Introduction
slides.notes: Moving on, these hardware instructions are atomic, meaning they either execute completely or not at all—they cannot be interrupted midway. This property forms the foundation of hardware-based synchronization used in modern operating systems.

slides.title: Synchronization Hardware
slides.body:
Example
Example: Reading and writing a variable together as a single step
Variable
Reading
Writing
slides.notes: Now, consider reading and writing a variable. If these two operations are performed as a single atomic step, no other process can interrupt them in between. This prevents inconsistent data and avoids race conditions.

slides.title: Synchronization Hardware
slides.body:
Three Main Hardware Methods
Test-and-Set
Test a lock and set it to busy in a single atomic step
Compare-and-Swap
Update a value only if it matches the expected value
Block context switches so the critical section runs uninterrupted
Interrupt Disabling
slides.notes: Next, there are three common hardware methods for synchronization. Test-and-Set checks and locks a resource in one atomic operation. Compare-and-Swap updates a value only if it matches the expected value. Interrupt Disabling temporarily prevents context switches, allowing the critical section to execute without interruption.

slides.title: Hardware Support - Test-and-Set
slides.body:
Pseudocode
A special CPU instruction that reads a variable and sets it to true in one uninterruptible step:
def test_and_set(lock):
   old_value = lock       # save old value
   lock = True            # set lock busy
   return old_value       # return old value
# Usage as a lock:
while test_and_set(lock) == True:
   pass                   # wait if busy
# --- CRITICAL SECTION ---
lock = False               # release lock
Pseudocode
slides.notes:
Now, let's look at Test-and-Set. It's a special CPU instruction that checks the value of a lock and sets it to busy in one atomic operation. Since this happens without interruption, only one process can acquire the lock at a time, ensuring mutual exclusion.
CODENow, old_value = lock stores the current lock value. Then, lock = True marks the lock as busy in a single atomic step. The instruction returns old_value so the process knows whether the lock was free. The while loop keeps waiting if the returned value is True, and after the critical section, lock = False releases the lock for the next process.

slides.title: Hardware Support
slides.body:
Everyone else gets true back and keeps spinning until the lock is released
Using it as a Lock
slides.notes: Now, let's see how Test-and-Set works as a lock. If the lock is false, it means the resource is free. The test_and_set instruction returns false, immediately sets the lock to true, and the process enters the critical section. Any other process now receives true, indicating the lock is busy, so it keeps spinning until the lock is released.

slides.title: Hardware Support
slides.body:
Compare-and-Swap
An atomic instruction that updates a variable only if it still holds the expected value:
def compare_and_swap(cell, expected, new_value):
   original = cell            # save old value
   if cell == expected:       # if unchanged
       cell = new_value       # take the lock
   return original            # return old value
# Usage as a lock:
while compare_and_swap(lock, 0, 1) != 0:
   pass                       # wait if busy
# --- CRITICAL SECTION ---
lock = 0                       # release lock
Pseudocode
slides.notes:
Moving on, Compare-and-Swap is another atomic hardware instruction. It updates the lock only if its current value matches the expected value. If the lock is free, the process acquires it and enters the critical section. Otherwise, it keeps waiting until the lock becomes available.

CODENow, original = cell stores the current value of the lock. Next, if cell == expected checks whether the lock is still free. If the condition is true, cell = new_value updates the lock atomically and acquires it. The instruction then returns original so the process knows whether it obtained the lock. Finally, the while loop keeps checking until the lock becomes available, and after the critical section, lock = 0 releases the lock for other processes.

slides.title: Hardware Support
slides.body:
Compare-and-Swap
Only the process that sees lock == 0 swaps it to 1 and enters; the rest keep checking
slides.notes: Next, with Compare-and-Swap, only the process that finds the lock value as 0 can change it to 1 and enter the critical section. All other processes keep checking until the lock is released, ensuring that only one process enters at a time.

slides.title: Hardware Support
slides.body:
Disabling Interrupts
No other process can be scheduled until it turns them back on
A context switch only happens because of an interrupt (like the CPU timer). So a process can just turn interrupts off before its critical section
How the Kernel Uses It:
disable_interrupts() # Stop CPU timer / hardware interrupts
  # ---- CRITICAL SECTION ----
enable_interrupts() # Allow interrupts again
Pseudocode
slides.notes:
Finally, another approach is disabling interrupts. Before entering the critical section, a process temporarily turns off interrupts, preventing the operating system from performing a context switch. This allows the process to finish its critical section without interruption, after which interrupts are enabled again.


Now, let's understand this approach. The kernel first calls disable_interrupts() to prevent context switches before entering the critical section. After completing the critical operation, it calls enable_interrupts() so the system can resume normal interrupt handling and scheduling.

slides.title: Disabling Interrupts
slides.body:
Limitations
Only works on single-processor systems - on a multicore CPU, other cores keep running
Unsafe for user programs - a process could disable interrupts and never re-enable them, freezing the system
Important interrupts can be missed while they're off
slides.notes: However, disabling interrupts has several limitations.1 It works only on single-processor systems, since other CPU cores continue running in multicore systems. 2 It's also unsafe for user programs, as failing to re-enable interrupts could freeze the system. 3 Additionally, important hardware interrupts may be delayed or missed while interrupts are disabled.
